source: Kolodner (1993) Introduction to the special issue on case-based reasoning. Machine Learning 10:195-199
finding: Kolodner defines CBR as reasoning from remembered experiences and says memory has two parts: putting cases in, and recalling them later. She calls this the indexing problem.
numbers: No experiments; an editorial introduction to a special issue.
quote: Remembering has two parts: integrating cases or experiences into memory when they happen and recalling them in appropriate situations later on.
limits: Founding statement only; it is a position, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: A stored record is only as good as its labels. S9 must write the situation labels at write time, not only the lesson.

source: Kolodner (1993) Introduction to the special issue on case-based reasoning. Machine Learning 10:195-199
finding: Indexing has two sub-problems. At store time, give each experience labels that say when it applies. At recall time, elaborate the new situation until it carries the labels it would have had in memory.
numbers: Two capabilities decide performance: how well the system anticipates a case's future usefulness, and how well it assesses a new situation.
limits: Theory; no measured comparison of indexing schemes in this text.
agent_relevance: Write S9 labels as 'when this applies' (class, trap, helper-problem), and make S1/S2 produce the same label fields for the new problem.

source: Kolodner (1993) Introduction to the special issue on case-based reasoning. Machine Learning 10:195-199
finding: Failure cases are worth storing. If the system can explain a failure it can index the case so the failure is recognised before it happens again. If it can also find the repair, the repair is stored in the case and indexed so it can be recalled as a fix.
limits: Requires an explanation step for failures; without it a failure record has no good index.
agent_relevance: S9 should store failures with the failing output and the repair that worked (links to G2), not only successes.

source: Kolodner (1993) Introduction to the special issue on case-based reasoning. Machine Learning 10:195-199
finding: Cases can be re-indexed after use: if a recalled case proved inappropriate, change its labels so it is not recalled in such situations; if a missed case should have been used, add the missing label.
limits: Described as a research direction in 1993, no numbers.
agent_relevance: Our class pass-rate and agreement records are a crude re-indexing signal; per-record helped/hurt counts would be the next step.

source: Kolodner (1993) Introduction to the special issue on case-based reasoning. Machine Learning 10:195-199
finding: Case admission should be controlled. A new case belongs only if it lets the reasoner do something it could not, or do something faster. Otherwise it adds storage and may slow retrieval.
limits: Stated as a principle; the measured version is Smyth and Keane 1995 (see subfield 01).
agent_relevance: Matches the 'schema must pay for itself' rule (G7) applied to memory: write a record only if it changes future behaviour.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Aamodt and Plaza state the representation problem as three choices: what to store in a case, how to structure the case content, and how to organise and index the case memory. A typical case is richer than a feature vector with a class label.
quote: The representation problem in CBR is primarily the problem of deciding what to store in a case ...
limits: A review; no new data.
agent_relevance: Names the three decisions S9 has to settle: content, structure, index.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Definition used in the field: a case is a problem situation that was experienced and captured so it can be reused. The retained case holds problem descriptors and solution, and can also hold an explanation of why the solution works, or the solving method (derivational reuse).
numbers: CASEY keeps all observed features plus the causal explanation of the diagnosis and the list of heart-failure model states with evidence; those states are the primary indices.
limits: Examples come from 1980s systems; no accuracy numbers are given in this review.
agent_relevance: A record can carry three optional layers: problem+solution, a justification, and the method trace. We currently keep one lesson line; the justification layer is the missing piece.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Dynamic memory model (Schank, Kolodner, CYRUS). Memory is a tree of generalized episodes. Each holds norms (features shared by all its cases), cases, and indices (features that discriminate between cases). An index is a name-value pair pointing to one case or one sub-episode. Retrieval finds the episode with most matching norms, then follows indices.
numbers: When two cases share an index, a new generalized episode is created automatically to separate them.
limits: Indexing cost grows with case count; most systems cap the number of cases or index depth.
agent_relevance: A hierarchy of 'problem class' (norms) with discriminating features below is a design option for S9 memory if flat retrieval stops working.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Category-exemplar model (Porter, Bareiss, PROTOS). Cases are exemplars of categories. Three link types: remindings (feature to case or category), exemplar links (category to cases, sorted by prototypicality), and difference links (case to near neighbour that differs in few features). Generalisation is done cautiously or not at all.
limits: Built for classification (audiology); other task types may not map onto categories.
agent_relevance: Supports storing concrete instances with 'differs from X in Y' links rather than only abstract lessons.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Retain step: update the case base whatever way the problem was solved. Decide what to extract (problem descriptors, solution, explanation, solving method), how to index, and how to integrate. Failures from the Revise step can be kept as separate failure cases or inside the case, so a reminding can point to a past similar failure.
limits: Description, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Directly describes S9. A failure record should be a first-class record kind.

source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches. AI Communications 7(1):39-59
finding: Index selection is a knowledge-acquisition problem. The trivial answer is to index on all input features (syntax-based memory methods). CASEY uses two-step indexing: primary general causal states, then remaining features. CBR-Talk filters features by matching all cases in parallel.
limits: No comparison numbers in the review.
agent_relevance: Labels should be chosen by what is useful for discrimination, not all features. For us: class, operator used, trap type, and outcome.

source: Aha, Kibler & Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms. Machine Learning 6:37-66
finding: Instance-based learning keeps raw instances and no abstractions. IB1 stores every instance and classifies by nearest neighbour. IB2 stores only instances IB1 misclassified. IB3 adds a record of each stored instance's classification success and drops instances that do poorly (a noise filter).
limits: Attribute-vector cases with a class label only; classification tasks; not the rich cases of CBR. Authors say C4 wins where concepts align with attribute axes (Voting).
agent_relevance: Keeping 7-30% of cases, selected by their own track record, matched or beat keeping all of them. Supports a per-record success tally and pruning in S9.

source: Aha, Kibler & Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms. Machine Learning 6:37-66
finding: IB2 is more sensitive to noise than IB1 because it keeps only the cases it got wrong, and noisy cases are almost always wrong. IB3's success-record filter fixes this.
numbers: With 10% attribute noise in the artificial domain, 20 of IB2's 76 saved instances (26.3%) were noisy; the average across trials at that noise level was 28.3% of saved instances noisy. IB3 degraded more slowly with noise than IB2 or IB1 (Figure 11, 50 trials).
limits: Slightly lower accuracy than IB1 when no noise exists. Artificial domain plus a few real-world sets.
agent_relevance: 'Store only failures' is dangerous when failure labels are noisy (our own graders and LLM judges are). Keep a track record per stored case before trusting it.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento formalises a case as a triple (state, action, reward): the task, the plan, and whether it succeeded. Non-parametric memory just appends the triple and reads by SimCSE cosine similarity. Parametric memory also trains a Q-function that scores how useful a case is for a state. Only the final-step triple of each trajectory is written, to keep the bank compact.
numbers: Planner GPT-4.1, executor o4-mini (o3 for GAIA). Bank starts empty.
limits: Binary reward only; single bank design per run; no ablation of triple fields themselves.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to a minimal S9 record: task, attempt, pass/fail. Final-step-only writes avoid duplicates.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Number of retrieved cases K matters: more is not better. On the seven DeepResearcher datasets the average peaked at K=4 and was flat or slightly lower for larger K.
quote: The paper says CBR benefits from a small high-quality memory, unlike few-shot prompting.
limits: One benchmark family, one planner/executor pair; differences between K=1 and K=32 are under 1 point.
agent_relevance: Show the agent 1 to 4 records, not a dump. Retrieved record count should be a capped parameter.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Case memory adds a gain on top of planning and tools. On DeepResearcher, Memento without CBR scored 59.9 F1 / 72.2 PM and with CBR 66.6 / 80.4. On HLE, 22.2/17.4 became 26.7/24.4. On SimpleQA, 81.0/89.7 became 84.7/95.0.
numbers: Gain from CBR: DeepResearcher +6.7 F1 / +8.2 PM; HLE +4.5 / +7.0; SimpleQA +3.7 / +5.3. Table 5, planner GPT-4.1, executor o4-mini.
limits: Authors flag possible data contamination on DeepResearcher. No confidence intervals reported. Single runs.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a (task, plan, outcome) bank gives additive gains over a scaffold, but at modest size.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Learning curve over five passes on DeepResearcher: the case bank saturates quickly (about 3k training items). Parametric case selection beats non-parametric, and both beat no CBR, but the margins shrink.
numbers: Iter 1 to 5 accuracy: no CBR 78.65, 80.93, 82.62, 83.53, 84.47; non-parametric 79.84, 81.87, 83.09, 84.03, 84.85; parametric 80.46, 82.84, 84.10, 84.85, 85.44. At iteration 5 the gap to no CBR is 0.4 (non-param) and 1.0 (param) points.
limits: Small gaps at iteration 5; no variance reported. The no-CBR arm also improves (it re-runs the same tasks), so part of the curve is not from memory.
agent_relevance: Do not expect memory to compound without limit; plan to measure the gap against a same-iteration no-memory arm.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Headline results: top-1 on GAIA validation at 87.88% (Pass@3, three iterations storing both successful and failed trajectories), 79.40% on the GAIA test set using the bank built on validation. Reports 4.7 to 9.6 absolute point gains from case memory on out-of-distribution tasks.
numbers: HLE 24.4% PM vs GPT-5 25.32%; SimpleQA 95.0% PM.
limits: Test set used a bank built on validation tasks; Pass@3 is a generous metric; cost of planner plus executor stack not equal to a plain model (G7).
agent_relevance: Both successes and failures were stored. Shows the record kind is workable; does not isolate the value of failures.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: ReasoningBank stores distilled strategy items, not raw trajectories. Each memory item has three fields: a title (short identifier), a one-sentence description, and a content body (reasoning steps, decision rationale, operational insight). Items are induced from both successes and failures, with success/failure labelled by an LLM judge.
numbers: Retrieval is embedding similarity; new items extracted after each task.
quote: Each memory item specifies three components: (i) a title ... (ii) a description ... and (iii) the content
limits: Success labels come from an LLM judge (accuracy 72.7% against ground truth on WebArena-Shopping).
agent_relevance: A ready schema for the S9 lesson: title, one-line description for retrieval, body for use.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Strategy-level items beat raw-trajectory memory and success-only workflow memory. Overall WebArena success rate with Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5, Synapse (raw trajectories) 42.1, AWM (workflows from successes) 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8. Steps per task fell from 9.7 (no memory) to 8.3.
numbers: WebArena 684 tasks (Shopping 187, Admin 182, Gitlab 180, Reddit 106, Multi 29). Gains over no memory across three backbones: +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 points overall.
limits: Single benchmark family plus SWE-Bench-Verified and Mind2Web; LLM-judge labels; authors are the ReasoningBank team.
agent_relevance: Supports abstracting a record into a strategy rather than replaying the trace.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Failures help only if the schema can use them. Adding failed trajectories lifted ReasoningBank on WebArena-Shopping from 46.5 to 49.7, but moved Synapse only from 40.6 to 41.7 and lowered AWM from 44.4 to 42.2.
numbers: No-memory baseline 39.0 on that split. Figure 7.
limits: One split (Shopping), one backbone (Gemini-2.5-flash).
agent_relevance: Writing failures into the same format as successes can hurt (AWM). A failure record needs its own field: what went wrong, what to avoid.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Fewer retrieved items worked best: one item gave the top score and more items lowered it.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 39.0; 1 item 49.7; 2 items 46.5; 3 items 45.5; 4 items 44.4.
quote: The relevance and quality of memory are more crucial than sheer quantity.
limits: One split, one model.
agent_relevance: Same message as Memento K: retrieve one or two records.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: ReasoningBank is reported to hold up when the judge is wrong. The LLM judge was 72.7% accurate on WebArena-Shopping; the paper then injected additional judge errors and scores stayed in a narrow band.
numbers: Success-rate curve across judge accuracy 100% down to 50% stays roughly between 47.6 and 52.4 on Shopping (read from chart text, approximate).
limits: Numbers read from a chart text dump; treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Strategy-style records may survive noisy outcome labels. Still, our G3 rule (real checks) should set the outcome field.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-based reasoning for retrieval augmented generation in LLMs for legal question answering
finding: CBR-RAG defines a case as a tuple c = <Q, S, E, A>: question, support text, entities extracted from the support, and answer. The authors add S and E to the usual problem-solution pair to give the LLM grounded context and extra indexing keys.
numbers: Casebase: 2,124 LLM-generated QA pairs from the Australian Open Legal Corpus; 1,183 (57%) had no reference to legal acts, so act names were not usable as index terms.
limits: Generated Q/A pairs, not real cases; Mistral-7B generator; test set only 32 cases built from pairs of parent cases.
agent_relevance: Shows a case can need a third element (support/evidence) beyond problem and solution; for us the equivalent is the failing output or check result.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-based reasoning for retrieval augmented generation in LLMs for legal question answering
finding: Case parts used for retrieval matter. A hybrid similarity over question, support and entity embeddings with weights [0.25, 0.40, 0.35] and AnglE embeddings, k=3, gave the best retrieval F1 among the combinations tested (BERT, LegalBERT, AnglE; question-only, support-only, entity-only, hybrid).
numbers: Retrieval test: 32 test cases, each with 2 parent cases treated as relevant; k from primes between 1 and 37.
limits: Tiny test set; weights not tuned beyond the options listed.
agent_relevance: Index on several fields of the record, not on one text blob.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-based reasoning for retrieval augmented generation in LLMs for legal question answering
finding: Putting the full case in the prompt beat putting only the support text, and CBR-RAG beat no retrieval, but the gain is small. Cosine similarity of answer to reference: no RAG 0.8967; best CBR-RAG (hybrid AnglE, k=3, full case) 0.9141, about a 1.94% gain.
numbers: Other cells: k=1 Hybrid BERT full case 0.9068, support-only 0.8986; k=3 AnglE support-only 0.9092. Significant vs No-RAG and vs hybrid LegalBERT k=3 at 95% (one-tailed t-test); vs hybrid BERT k=1 at 90%.
limits: The no-RAG baseline is already high because the model knows the law; metric is embedding cosine, not correctness; 32 test items.
agent_relevance: Whole-record context beat a fragment, but effect is under 2 points on a weak metric.

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: Automated data science by empowering LLMs with case-based reasoning. ICML
finding: DS-Agent keeps two banks. A human-insight bank holds text insights from Kaggle winning reports and GPT-3.5-summarised top notebooks (12 competitions, top-10 reports and top-10 notebooks each). An agent bank holds (task description, working Python script) pairs added whenever a run improves test performance.
numbers: Development stage: GPT-4 reaches 100% success over 12 tasks. Deployment stage, one-pass rate over 18 tasks: DS-Agent 85% (GPT-3.5) and 99% (GPT-4) vs best baseline 56% and 60%; Mixtral-8x7b-Instruct 6% to 31%.
limits: Authors' own task suite; baselines are zero-shot and one random example.
agent_relevance: Strongest published case for storing (task, working solution) pairs and retrieving by task description.

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: Automated data science by empowering LLMs with case-based reasoning. ICML
finding: Case form matters. A paired (example task, solution script) case beat free-text insights as the thing to reuse. The paper calls this homogeneous versus heterogeneous cases and reports the paired form better on nearly all tasks.
numbers: Figure 6a (per-task bars; no single average in the text I read).
quote: learning from the homogeneous case (i.e., an example task and one of its solutions) leads to better performance than from the heterogeneous case (i.e., textual solution insights)
limits: I did not extract exact per-task numbers; only direction is certain.
agent_relevance: Argues for keeping a concrete worked example in the record, not only an abstract lesson. This pulls against ReasoningBank's strategy-only format, so test both.

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: Automated data science by empowering LLMs with case-based reasoning. ICML
finding: Revising the ranking of retrieved cases using the last run's execution feedback helped. Average best rank over 12 development tasks (lower is better), GPT-4: full DS-Agent 2.08, without ReviseRank 2.58, without CBR (no human insights) 3.41.
numbers: Five repeat trials. Retrieval uses cosine similarity of embeddings, k=5, T=5 iterations.
limits: Ranks among the compared agents, not absolute scores.
agent_relevance: Retrieval should be re-ranked by the actual failing output (G2), not fixed at the start.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners. AAAI
finding: ExpeL stores two things at once: whole successful trajectories (retrieved by task similarity as examples) and a list of natural-language insights extracted from success/failure pairs and success lists, edited by ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE operations. Insights with zero importance are dropped.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%; WebShop 37% vs 38% (score 0.675 vs 0.67). Full ExpeL beats both.
limits: gpt-3.5-turbo agent, gpt-4 for insight extraction; three environments.
agent_relevance: Instances and abstractions help different task types; keep both fields in a record and let the task class decide which to show.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners. AAAI
finding: Ablations on what is stored and how it is retrieved (label-to-number mapping is from a garbled text extract, so treat as probable). HotpotQA: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, insights with reflections 29.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld: ReAct 40.0, retrieve by reasoning similarity 48.5, random sampled trajectories 42.5, task-similarity ExpeL 59.0.
numbers: Standard errors range 0.3 to 2.1 points.
limits: Column/label alignment inferred; a second reading of the PDF table image is needed before quoting.
agent_relevance: Task-similarity retrieval clearly beat random and reasoning-similarity retrieval in ALFWorld.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried & Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent Workflow Memory stores reusable sub-routines induced from successful runs, with example-specific values replaced by placeholders so they generalise. Online use induces workflows from the agent's own test-time successes in a stream.
numbers: Relative gains over the baseline: 24.6% (Mind2Web step success rate) and 51.1% (WebArena success rate); WebArena total success rate 35.5 with GPT-4; reported to beat agents given 14 human-written workflows by 7.9%.
limits: Workflows come from successes only, and the paper warns that incorrect workflows can degrade performance; ReasoningBank later shows AWM falling when failures are added.
agent_relevance: Parameterise stored procedures (placeholders). Only store workflows whose outcome was verified (G3).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: LLM agents show experience-following: the more similar a new task's input is to a retrieved record's input, the more similar the agent's output is to that record's output. Add-all memory therefore copies past errors.
numbers: Four agents. Task success/accuracy with fixed memory vs add-all: RegAgent 67.53 vs 55.48; EHRAgent 16.75 vs 13.05; AgentDriver 40.11 vs 32.32; CIC-IoT 71.50 vs 59.90. Memory sizes 50 to 180 (fixed) vs 1,050 to 4,100 (add-all).
limits: One synthetic and three real agents; LLM backbones GPT-4o-mini and similar.
agent_relevance: Storing every run is worse than a small fixed good memory. Strong support for code-checked writes in S9.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Selective addition works only with a good quality filter. A strict (human-level) evaluator beat the fixed memory on all four agents; coarse automatic evaluators were mixed and sometimes worse than fixed memory.
limits: The strict evaluator uses ground truth, which an agent does not have at run time.
agent_relevance: Quality of the outcome label decides memory quality; G3/G5 (code-checked pass on held-out data) is the closest thing available to a strict label.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Errors compound: compared with a variant using the same retrieved examples but with ground-truth outputs, add-all and coarse selective addition show a growing performance gap over the task stream. History-based deletion (remove records that are retrieved often yet whose later tasks score badly) can beat even the error-free baseline on AgentDriver with a strict evaluator.
numbers: Misaligned experience replay: records that pass the quality filter can still mislead the current task.
limits: Deletion help varied with the reliability of the evaluator; under task-distribution shift, results were mixed (EHRAgent deletion underperformed).
agent_relevance: Keep per-record retrieved-N-times, helped-M-times counts and prune on them, as IB3 did in 1991.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: Storing curated, short strategy notes beat storing raw past input-output pairs. On AIME 2024 Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored 26.7% with full-history appending and 50.0% with Dynamic Cheatsheet variants; GPT-4o went from a 20.0% baseline to 6.7% with full history and 40.0% with DC-RS.
numbers: GPQA-Diamond, Claude: baseline 59.6%, dynamic retrieval of verbatim past pairs (DR) 63.6%, DC-RS 68.7%; GPT-4o only 57.1% to 58.1%. Game of 24 (GPT-4o) from about 10% to 99% after it stored and reused a Python solution.
limits: Small question sets (AIME has 30 questions per year, so each question is 3.3 points); GPT-4o gained little on GPQA.
agent_relevance: Raw history hurts, retrieved raw pairs help a little, curated notes help most. Supports a compact record over a full transcript.

source: Hatalis et al. (2025) Review of case-based reasoning for LLM agents
finding: A review that gives a case for LLM agents as a tuple c = (P, S, O, M): problem features, solution actions, outcome metrics, and metadata (time, environment, provenance). It proposes dense embeddings plus sparse feature indices with coarse-to-fine retrieval, and uses Richter's knowledge containers (vocabulary, cases, similarity, adaptation).
numbers: No new experiments (zero 'we conduct' statements in the text I read). The listed benefit claims, e.g. higher user trust, are not tied to specific numbers in the cited text.
limits: Theory and synthesis only; claims about effects are not measured by the authors.
agent_relevance: A ready-made field list for S9: problem features, solution, outcome, and metadata (when, which model, which budget).

source: Feng et al. (2023) Case repositories: Towards case-based reasoning for AI alignment
finding: Case repositories for AI alignment. A case is a seed question, plus expert-elicited key dimensions (20 legal experts in groups of 3-4 produced dimensions such as location, data collection, minors involved, nature of data, terms of service), plus LLM-generated variations along those dimensions, plus public judgments.
numbers: No measured accuracy; process proposal.
limits: A proposal paper without evaluation.
agent_relevance: Shows dimensions as the case-representation layer: name the axes of difference between cases. Useful for S2 class labels, not tested.
